real_s1.explanation: Within its top classes, which are mostly road vehicles, this unit is most clearly driven by how sharp the main subject is. It is much more active when the vehicle or object is in crisp focus than when it is slightly blurry. This preference held strongly on new photos and is particular to this unit, since the similar units do not share it. There are weaker tendencies toward rightward-facing side views, a subject filling much of the frame, and untinted photos rather than warm-tinted ones, but none of these were reliable on new photos.

real_s2.explanation: The unit responds most to vehicles and vehicle-like objects (trucks, buses, cars, forklifts, plus parking meters, grilles and the like) when the subject is sharply in focus. Sharp versus slightly blurry is the one property that is unusual for this layer (98th percentile), is not shared by the similar units, and held on new photos (95th percentile). There are weaker tendencies toward right-facing, side-on, large, level subjects with no warm color cast. These did not replicate at an unusual level on the new photos, so they are not confidently particular to this unit.

real_s3.explanation: The unit responds to vehicles and similar man-made objects (cars, trucks, buses, plus things like parking meters, lamps and drills) when the main subject is sharp and in focus. Sharpness is the only property that held up on new photos: the unit is much more active on sharp subjects than on slightly blurry ones, and this is unusual for its layer (similar units are not unusual there). The apparent preferences for right-facing subjects and for untinted color did not replicate. Weaker trends toward large, partly cut-off, single main subjects are not unusual for the layer.

null_s1.explanation: The unit responds most strongly to vehicle classes (cars, trucks, buses, emergency vehicles) and some vehicle-like or boxy objects such as parking meters, tape players, and power drills. Within those classes, none of the photo properties asked about reliably changes its activity. The original sample suggested preferences for right-facing subjects, sharp focus, and untinted photos. None of these held up on new photos: d shrank to near zero and the percentiles fell to ordinary levels. Other rows, such as preferences for large, cut-off single subjects over scenes with no main subject, were never unusual for the layer. The unit is best described simply as a vehicle-class detector with no confirmed preference for orientation, framing, lighting, tint, or sharpness.

null_s2.explanation: The unit is most active on road vehicles and vehicle-like objects: pickups, wagons, cabs, buses, trucks, forklifts, and related classes such as parking meters and grilles. Within those classes, none of the photo properties asked about reliably changes its activity. The only rows at or above the 95th percentile were sharp versus slightly blurry and facing right versus toward the camera. Neither held on new photos (percentiles 45 and 67), and the colour-tint and facing-right versus no-direction rows also fell to ordinary levels. All other rows were below 95 to begin with. So I can't attribute any of the asked-about properties (facing direction, framing, sharpness, tint, tilt, lighting) to this unit specifically. Its distinctive selectivity, if any, lies outside these questions.

null_s3.explanation: The unit is most active on road vehicles of all kinds (pickups, wagons, cabs, trucks, buses, vans, sports cars, jeeps), plus a few vehicle-like or vehicle-adjacent objects (parking meter, grille, power drill, tape player, table lamp). Within these classes, none of the photo properties asked about reliably changes its activity. The apparent preferences in the first sample were sharp over blurry subjects, right-facing over head-on views, and untinted over warm-tinted color. All four were checked on new photos and none held, falling to ordinary percentiles. The remaining rows were weak to begin with. So no facing, framing, lighting, tint or sharpness preference can be confidently attributed to this unit.
